recall.a: Cannabis users were about twice as likely to commit violence (two and a half times among psychiatric patients) and about one and a half times as likely to be victims. But it is only a link. Alcohol, other drugs and hard lives often come with cannabis use and could explain part of it. The link was also smaller in studies that followed people over time.

cards.title: Brain disorders may age the brain in different ways
cards.body: A computer can look at a brain scan and guess how old its owner is. In a large study, people with dementia, addiction and some psychiatric conditions had brains that looked older than their real age. Each condition seemed to leave its own pattern.
cards.evidence: single study · 2,698 people with conditions vs 45,900 controls · structural MRI · correlational

sections.text:
Show a computer thousands of brain scans and it learns what a brain looks like at 30, at 50 and at 70. Give it a new scan and it can guess the owner's age. Sometimes the guess is higher than the person's real age. This study is about that gap.

The gap has a name: predictive age difference, or PAD. It is the age the scan suggests minus the person's real age. A positive PAD means the brain looks older than expected. A team led by Shile Qi at the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics in China asked one question: do different brain conditions make the brain look older in different ways?

They used structural MRI. This kind of scan shows the brain's shape and tissue, not its activity. They took scans of 45,900 people without these conditions from several databases and used them as the comparison group. Then they looked at 2,698 people with one of these conditions: ADHD, autism, alcohol or tobacco addiction, Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment (memory and thinking problems milder than dementia), schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or major depression.

The strongest link was with Alzheimer's and mild cognitive impairment. These brains looked the most 'older than their years'. Addiction and the psychiatric conditions also had higher PAD. ADHD and autism showed no overall difference.

Things got more interesting when the team checked the brain region by region. Each condition seemed to leave its own pattern. One area stood out across many disorders: the prefrontal cortex, at the very front of the brain. In the psychiatric disorders, the frontal and temporal lobes (the front and the sides of the brain) looked older. In dementia, it was the frontal cortex and the occipital cortex at the back.

Addiction had a different pattern again. Two large systems of linked brain areas looked older: the default mode network and the salience network. So did two deep structures, the putamen and the thalamus.

The team also checked which genes were active in each condition, and found differences there too. This hints that each pattern may come from its own biological process, not from one general wear and tear. In the authors' words, each disorder seems to leave its own 'signatures on the brain aging clock'. They hope PAD could one day help find biomarkers, which are measurable signs of a disease, and point to the biology behind these conditions.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This study is correlational. It does not show that these conditions make the brain age faster. Also, psychiatric disorders and addiction often happen together, so it is hard to separate the effect of one from the other. And a brain's 'age' here is a computer's guess from a scan, not a direct measure of aging.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A brain can look older than its owner, and where it looks older may hint at which illness is involved.

recall.q: What does PAD measure, and what did the study find when it looked at PAD region by region?
recall.a: PAD is the gap between the age a brain scan suggests and the person's real age; a positive PAD means the brain looks older than expected. Region by region, each condition had its own pattern: psychiatric disorders in the frontal and temporal lobes, dementia in the frontal and occipital cortex, and addiction in networks like the default mode network and deep areas like the thalamus. The study is correlational, so it does not show the conditions cause this.

cards.title: Depression changes which faces a child looks at
cards.body: As children become more depressed, the faces they look at change. But how they change depends on the mother. Children of depressed mothers get stuck on sad faces. Other children slowly stop looking at happy ones.
cards.evidence: single study · n=242 children and their mothers · followed 2 years, tested every 6 months · eye tracking

sections.text:
Every six months for two years, a child sat in front of a screen while a camera tracked their eyes. Two faces appeared side by side. One showed no feeling. The other was happy, sad or angry. The camera recorded which face the child looked at, and for how long.

The study followed 242 children and their mothers. It was run by researchers at Binghamton University in New York. Some of the mothers had a history of major depression. Some did not. At each visit, the team also measured the children's depressive symptoms: signs like low mood and loss of interest.

The question behind the study is old. We already knew that depressed people tend to look longer at sad faces. But that link was weak, and nobody knew which came first. Does a pull toward sadness lead to depression? Or does depression create the pull? By testing the same children again and again, the team could check both directions over time. They say no one had done this with children before.

The results reported here point one way: symptoms rose first, and attention changed after. And the change was not the same for every child. It depended on the family.

In children whose mothers had been depressed, rising symptoms meant more attention to sad faces. The lab's director, Brandon Gibb, explains it simply: these children lose the ability to pull their attention away from the sad things around them.

In children whose mothers had no depression, something else happened. Rising symptoms did not pull them toward sad faces. Instead, they looked less at happy ones. Gibb sees this as depression breaking a protective habit. Noticing happy faces seems to help protect a child. Depression slowly takes that habit away.

So there may be two paths. For one group, sadness gets harder to ignore. For the other, joy gets easier to miss. From the outside, the two may look the same. Inside, they are different.

Why would the mother's history matter? The lead author, Kelly Gair, offers one possible reason, and calls it a guess. A child of a depressed mother may see many sad faces at home. Those faces become extra important to that child. Then, when the child becomes depressed, their attention gets stuck there.

The team studied children on purpose. At this age, most weak spots are still forming, so you can catch them early, before they become fixed. The team is now following the same children into their teenage years, when the risk of depression rises. They want to know if these early eye patterns predict who later gets a diagnosis.

sections.label: See it in your life
sections.text:
When you feel low, notice where your eyes go in a crowd: toward the tired faces, or away from the smiling ones?

The two paths may need different help. One person needs to loosen their grip on sadness. Another needs to win back their attention to good things.

A child of a depressed parent may carry a different kind of risk, not just a bigger one.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one study of 242 families. It shows that symptoms and attention changed together over time. It does not yet show that these eye patterns lead to a later diagnosis; the follow-up into the teenage years will test that. The idea that sad faces at home explain the difference is the authors' guess. The study did not test it. Earlier links between depression and attention to sad faces were weak.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Depression does not only add sadness to what we see. Sometimes it quietly takes the happy faces away.

recall.q: As depressive symptoms rose, how did attention change in children of depressed mothers compared with children of non-depressed mothers?
recall.a: Children of depressed mothers looked more and more at sad faces and got stuck on them. Children of non-depressed mothers did not look more at sad faces. Instead, they looked less at happy faces, losing a habit that seems to protect them.
